Hospice

By: Stenette Grosskopf | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Holistic end-of-life care is about much more than just dispensing the right medication...

Unique Selling Point:
Many people associate Hospice with death, and by saying "yes" to Hospice they feel they're saying "yes" to death, but this is a perception that needs to change. Hospice is about much more than just dispensing medication and keeping the patient comfortable until they die. The organisation wants to be a part of the entire journey of someone being diagnosed with a terminal disease. The Organisation employs doctors, nurses, social workers, psychologists and spiritual councillors that can give holistic care to the patient and the entire family. Patients may be treated at their in-patient facilities or may be supported whilst being cared for in their own homes. Coming to terms with a terminal illness places a lot of stress on the entire family and this is where the emotional en physical support of Hospice staff becomes invaluable.

Summary:
Hospice provides all-round holistic care for the terminally ill and their families. Although most Medical Aids cover palliative care as part of their plans, Hospice relies on donor funding as many of their patients come from previously disadvantaged backgrounds. They don't turn anyone away and offer the same professional high-quality of care to everyone, irrespective of their financial position. But funding is drying up. Hospice only gets about 10% of its funding from Government and for the rest they rely on the public and corporate world. Int he past 2 years 10 in-patient facilities have closed down because of a lack of funding. Hospice Wits (with satellite branch, Soweto) is no different. The Soweto branch's in-patient unit was closed down in 2018, but the effects on the community was devastating. So, this year the unit was re-launched, but it's future is hanging in the balance.

Against this backdrop we meet the dedicated nurses and staff of Hospice and the invaluable services they offer. We speak to patients and their families who simply would not have coped without this assistance.

Further information:
Earnest Eric Barnard: A story of courage Earnest is a gentleman in his 50’s who was diagnosed with tongue cancer in October 2018. He has had a harrowing life journey filled with having to overcome many challenges. He is one of the many courageous members of the Hospice community in care. Sister Mel Griggs has been visiting Barnard where he stays with his Niece in Westdene, since he was diagnosed. Sr Mel has shared general guidelines on how to cope as a family unit with illness while also assisting with medication helping Earnest to be more comfortable and pain free.

Kevin Gous: His mother passed away in 2017. “Sr Mel from HospiceWits came and see to see us often – she was good for my mother but also good for us. She was a good caretaker but also therapeutic person to us. She would give us hugs to make us feel like we were family. We would not have made it through if we did not have HospiceWits”

Kune Sithole: Her brother has cancer and being a pensioner she doesn't have the financial means to look after him. He is currently at Hospice Soweto In-Patient Unit. She says everyone refused to help and take him, until she found hospice. It has been a great relief. He is comfortable and happy. She says it has made A LOT of difference.

These are some of the stories of families that have been helped by Hospice. The real heroes are the staff, the nurses who spend their lives giving. Houghton: Sr Notombi and Sr Francis and Soweto: Sr Maria and Sr Rachel.

Hospice Wits Soweto has 4 Registered nurses and 10 Community Workers for homecare who at this moment are caring for approximately 233 patients and families (that is over 50 patients per nurse). The Houghton team looks after around 300 patients. They also also have a re-furbished in patient unit which can accommodate around 11 patients at a time for short stays with 2 rooms dedicated to long term stays.
We have partnerships with some local churches who offer support, food parcels and care.

Script:


HOSPICE SCRIPT

Evy
My journey with my mom was a difficult journey.
VO
Evy Michalopoulos’s mother fell ill suddenly over Christmas and was diagnosed in January 2018 with stage 4 ovarian cancer. By then she was bedridden.
Evy
I took on the challenge to try and do as much as I could for my mom at home.

Devi: What was that like?

Evy: You know Devi it was very challenging because I have no experience in care-giving. I never knew the challenges that would come with it.
VO
It was only when she enlisted the support of Hospice Wits that Evy found the strength to break the news to her mother that her illness was terminal.
Evy
That was just such a sign [sic] of relief because I just thought, I don’t have to carry this burden any more on my own.
VO
Her mother passed away only five days later.
Evy
I wish my mom was able to have survived a little bit longer so that she could have been here at Hospice and been able to be given that love and support...and for us to be with her.


V/O
When Kevin Gouws’s mother Tersea (pr Tersha) was diagnosed with terminal cancer she made a plan...
Kevin
She came across Hospice and the primary reason she actually went for it is not for herself, she went for it for us. Because she wanted us to have as comfortable of a journey as possible.
V/O
The family’s experience of illness and death was transformed by the Hospice nurse who walked the journey with them.
Kevin
Most incredible person I’ve ever met. She made us feel like everything is alright.
One of my favourite memories that would be a complete curveball was getting home from class and you hear them laughing and then you walk into the room and you also start laughing because they’re doing that, where they can barely breathe because they’re laughing so hard. [Devi laughs]

Devi: And it doesn’t have to be traumatic.

Kevin: No, You felt like the last bit of time that we had left was much better than it would have been without them.
LINK
Being diagnosed with a terminal illness is daunting - for the patient and the family. But it's not a journey you ever have to walk alone.
Hlengiwe
Hospice is not all about death. It embraces life.
V/O
Sister Hlengiwe Dikeledi heads 8 dedicated palliative, registered Hospice Home Care Nurses.
Hlengiwe
As a hospice worker you are an angel sent from above.

Devi: You are.

That’s what I learnt because it’s not all about numbers. When I worked as a primary healthcare practitioner at a clinic we all count numbers, how many numbers you’ve seen. But here, if I can see one person a week and make a difference in this person’s life, and make a difference in this person’s family, it’s like you’ve done your lifetime work.
Jacqui
We are not there at the end. We are there at the beginning.
VO
Hospice Wits was founded 40 years ago as part of a global movement providing palliative care to patients, their families and communities through an incurable illness. Their care doesn’t end with medical services.
Jacqui
We work with the patient and when your family falls apart we bring in our counsellor, bring in our social worker. We’re there for you.
VO

CEO Jacqui Kaye oversees two branches, one in Houghton and one in Diepkloof, which serve the Johannesburg and greater Soweto communities.
Jacqui
We celebrate your life. We make sure that it’s pain-free, we make sure that your symptoms are controlled.
V/O
Sisters Maria Malahlela and Florina Xulu spend most of their days on the road, checking in on patients across Soweto.
Florina
This one I see every day. Then I’ve got another one in Pimville who I must see at least thrice. And the others I see twice.

Devi: That’s a lot!

That’s a lot.
V/O
I accompany the sisters on their home care rounds, as they check patients’ vitals, treat ailments, attend to personal hygiene and even help with daily tasks… all of it with love.
Maria
Devi: How long have you been with Hospice?

Whoo, before you were born…

Devi: Can’t be. How long have you been?

32 years.

Devi: Wow!
V/O
Johanna has a chronic lung disease and is HIV positive. Sister Maria has been looking after her for almost 5 years. Today is not a good day for Johanna, but our visit brings some comfort.
Maria
Devi: Do you feel like there’s this natural connection that you have?

Maria: A natural bond. A natural bond. You will never believe, these patients, these families, they become part and parcel of your family.
VO
To help families bear the burden, both branches of Hospice Wits also offer 24/7 in-patient care.
Jacqui
We bring them in to an in-patient unit for respite. So that the family can actually just have a week, couple of days, two weeks of sleeping, while 24 hour care is happening here in our in-patient unit.
V/O
And contrary to perceptions, being admitted is not a death sentence.
Maria

Devi: So, you do have examples where people come in in an ambulance, can’t walk, but leave walking?

Oh yes!

Devi: have you seen many miracles?

Maria: So many miracles. Some have gone back to work. Because we educate them on how to look after themselves. But of course yes when it’s time for you to die, we are so pleased because when you die in the unit or at home, we are there for you and the family is there. The thing that makes us strong is seeing our patients die with dignity and very peaceful and comfortable.
LINK
There are only four sisters who cover the area which stretches from Noordgesig to Lenasia. It’s not enough and right now they are supporting over 160 patients.
V/O
Running a non-profit is never easy and for Hospice, the situation is becoming precarious. Income from trusts and foundations, the hospice shops and patient billing is not enough to make ends meet.
jacqui
Early childhood development is where the money from CSI departments is going to, and it’s not going to healthcare anymore. For 10 years it has gotten worse. So we are drawing down probably millions from our investment on a regular basis. We can’t do that.
V/O
Salary cuts, retrenchments, and cost-cutting led to the closure of the Soweto in-patient unit in 2017 - but through sheer determination, the staff opened its doors again earlier this year.
Penny
We were seeing a need outside when we go to visit the patients at home. So, we came together, we sat down and we decided to contribute you know R100, R250…
V/O
Penny Mathe is the Hospice Soweto social worker, counselling patients as well as helping them access services. But since the unit reopened, she and all the staff are working multiple jobs.
Penny
We cook. We clean. I also man the reception at times. We are doing like everything because we are short staffed, we don’t have funds. So, we have to do everything.
V/O
“Everything” also means dipping into their own pockets.
Maria
You take whatever you have in your pocket so you can be able to buy some bread and nkomazi so that the person can have something to eat before she takes all her medication. Because at some homes you find that it’s so dry, there isn’t even crumbs of bread.
VO
They are facing restructuring and further retrenchments. But these extraordinary women are determined to keep giving.
Hlengiwe
To me, Hospice gave me that light to say you need to cherish life. Each and every moment you need to cherish it, because it can end at any time.
Penny
I don’t see myself anywhere else except here. This is where I belong.
Jacqui
We will not close our doors. We will not close the doors on what we do, which is offer that quality palliative care.

*** END ***


PROMO 1 11”
We meet the remarkable care workers from Hospice Wits in Johannesburg, a dedicated team you would most certainly want on your side when you’re faced with a difficult end-of-life journey.


PROMO 2 11”
Being diagnosed with a terminal illness puts huge amounts of stress on both, the patients and their loved ones. We meet the angels who keep families smiling till the end.


PROMO 3 11”
Hospice is about a lot more than just caring for terminally ill patients in their last days. It’s about looking after families and creating memories that will remain long after the patient’s final journey.

Kevin Gous: His mother passed away in 2017. “Sr Mel from HospiceWits came and see to see us often – she was good for my mother but also good for us. She was a good caretaker but also therapeutic person to us. She would give us hugs to make us feel like we were family. We would not have made it through if we did not have HospiceWits” Kune Sithole: Her brother has cancer and being a pensioner she doesn't have the financial means to look after him. He is currently at Hospice Soweto In-Patient Unit. She says everyone refused to help and take him, until she found hospice. It has been a great relief. He is comfortable and happy. She says it has made A LOT of difference. These are some of the stories of families that have been helped by Hospice. The real heroes are the staff, the nurses who spend their lives giving. Houghton: Sr Notombi and Sr Francis and Soweto: Sr Maria and Sr Rachel. Hospice Wits Soweto has 4 Registered nurses and 10 Community Workers for homecare who at this moment are caring for approximately 233 patients and families (that is over 50 patients per nurse). The Houghton team looks after around 300 patients. They also also have a re-furbished in patient unit which can accommodate around 11 patients at a time for short stays with 2 rooms dedicated to long term stays. We have partnerships with some local churches who offer support, food parcels and care.
